title: Shooting Star over ESO Telescopes
caption: A shooting star over the ExTrA telescopes, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A shooting star flashes across the night sky towards the horizon of the Atacama Desert, above two of the three new ExTrA telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory. The telescopes sit more than 2000 meters above sea level and search for Earth-sized planets around M class stars, which are smaller than the Sun.
Despite the name, a shooting star is not a star at all. It is a small piece of rock or dust that burns up as it enters Earth's atmosphere. Before that happens, such a fragment is called a meteoroid.
These streaks are useful as well as pretty. By following the path and brightness of a meteoroid, scientists can trace its origin within the Solar System and learn its composition.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The camera records the meteor's whole path as a single streak, whereas the eye catches it only as a brief flash, and the exposure also gathers more starlight.

explore: If a meteoroid survives its fall through the atmosphere and reaches the ground, it becomes a meteorite. Meteorites are studied closely for what they reveal about the Solar System's past.
alt: A meteor streak crosses a starry sky above two telescope enclosures in the desert.
